opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think those two things are actually pretty tightly linked for us, maybe more than people realize. A lot of what METR does starts from the question of "what can these systems do right now?", and we try to answer it carefully, with tasks that look like real work, especially software engineering and research tasks, rather than multiple-choice benchmarks that saturate quickly. But a snapshot of current capabilities on its own isn't that useful for decision-making. What labs, policymakers, and the public want to know is: how worried should we be in six months, or two years? So the forecasting piece comes out of the measurement piece.

The time horizon work is a good example. We measured how long tasks take skilled humans, then looked at which tasks models could reliably complete, and summarized a model's capability as the length of task it succeeds at about half the time. That's a capability assessment of current models. Once you have a metric like that, consistent across many models over several years, you can plot it and see the trend, which has been surprisingly steady exponential growth, doubling roughly every several months. That trend then becomes a forecasting tool.

So I don't see it as a strict trade-off where we put x percent into forecasting and the rest into evaluation. Good forecasting depends on good measurement. If your measurements are noisy, saturated, or not tracking what matters, your extrapolations will be garbage. A lot of our effort goes into making the measurement trustworthy: thinking about task distributions, how messy or well-specified tasks are, how our tasks differ from real-world work, and whether we're eliciting the model's full capability.

That said, there are real tensions. For a pre-deployment evaluation of a specific model, the priority is getting the most accurate answer about that model, with things like elicitation and checking for sandbagging, under time pressure. For forecasting, you care more about consistency across models and time, even if a given task suite is imperfect, because you want an apples-to-apples trend. And forecasting forces uncomfortable questions about external validity: does our benchmark trend translate into real-world impact, like accelerating AI R&D? We've done work like the developer productivity study partly because benchmark extrapolations can diverge from what happens in practice, and we want to know when they do.

So the balance is something like: measurement is the foundation, forecasting is a big part of why the measurement matters, and we try to stay honest about the gap between "the line on our graph keeps going up" and "here's what will happen in the world."

r001.rationale: The response discusses measuring current model capabilities and forecasting, but does not say that current capabilities are themselves a subject of substantial disagreement.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think of those as pretty tightly coupled, honestly. The way I'd put it is that forecasting is really hard to do well if you don't have a solid handle on where things are right now, and you can't say much about where things are right now without some sense of the trajectory, because a single snapshot doesn't tell you that much on its own.

So a lot of what METR does is build evaluations: tasks that are meant to measure what models can actually do, especially on the kinds of things we care about, like autonomous software engineering, AI R&D, that sort of thing. And then the thing that makes those evaluations useful for forecasting is running them on a bunch of models over time, so you get a trend line rather than just a point. The time-horizon work is probably the clearest example of that, where the headline isn't really "model X can do a task that takes a human two hours," it's "that number has been doubling every several months, and here's what that implies if it keeps going."

I think the honest answer is that the current-capabilities side is where most of the effort goes, because that's the part you can do rigorously. Forecasting involves a lot more extrapolation and assumptions, and I'd want to be fairly humble about it. But I also think if you only do the measurement part and refuse to say anything about trends, you're sort of leaving the most decision-relevant part on the table. Policymakers and labs want to know not just "is this model dangerous today," but "how much warning do we get, and what should we be preparing for." So I see the capability assessment as the foundation, and the forecasting as a careful, caveated layer on top of it, rather than two separate projects competing for attention.

One thing I'd add is that there's a bit of a tension in there, because the evaluations that are easiest to run reliably aren't always the ones that best capture the capabilities that would matter for a forecast. So some of the balancing act is really about which tasks to build, and whether you're measuring something that will still be meaningful a couple of years out, or something that saturates and stops being informative.

r001.rationale: The response discusses measuring current capabilities and the limits of forecasting, but does not state that current AI capabilities are a subject of substantial disagreement.

astra-6.text:
I think those are closely related, but they’re different tasks. A lot of our work is about measuring what systems can do today, particularly whether they can carry out tasks autonomously over longer periods of time. And that’s useful even if you’re not trying to make a forecast: you want to understand what a model can actually accomplish, where it fails, and how much human assistance it needs.

But one motivation for developing those measurements is that we’d like to say something about where things are going. If you can evaluate successive models on a reasonably consistent scale, then you can start asking whether there’s a trend and what extrapolating it would imply.

The distinction I’d make is that a measurement of current capability doesn’t automatically give you a reliable forecast. You have to make additional assumptions about whether the trend will continue, whether your tasks remain representative, and whether something changes about how these systems are trained or used. So I see current capability assessment as a foundation for forecasting, while wanting to be explicit about the uncertainty that gets added when you move from one to the other.

r001.rationale: The response discusses measuring current AI capabilities and the limits of forecasting from those measurements, but it does not say that current capability is a subject of substantial disagreement.

sol-6.1.text:
I think of those as closely connected. If you want to forecast what AI systems will be able to do, you need a pretty good understanding of what they can do now, and you need measurements that you can compare over time.

A lot of the practical work is assessing current systems: designing tasks, checking that our evaluations actually measure what we care about, and understanding how much the results depend on the scaffolding or the amount of help we give a model. But one reason to do that work is to get a better picture of where things are going. Are systems becoming able to complete longer tasks? Are there particular capabilities that are improving quickly, or bottlenecks that seem persistent?

I would distinguish that from treating a trend as a reliable prediction. You can have a fairly solid measurement of current capabilities and still have substantial uncertainty about how it extrapolates. So I see current capability assessment as a foundation for forecasting, while trying to keep those different levels of uncertainty clear.

r001.rationale: The response discusses measuring current capabilities and uncertainty about extrapolating trends, but does not say that current system capabilities are themselves a subject of substantial disagreement.
